posts.body:
We have more buyer and lease leads than we can actually work right now.

1. Mostly new construction in San Antonio and Austin, plus out-of-state relocations coming in. The leads are warm but they need real vetting and nurturing before they're transaction ready.

2. Most of these buyers aren't buying tomorrow. They're buying in three months or six months. If you're the kind of agent who knows how to work a lead that isn't hot yet and turn it into a closed deal down the road, we have inventory for you.

3. The catch is real. They need patience and a system. You can't treat them like a hot buyer and expect to close in two weeks. You need to nurture. You need to follow up. You need to stay in front of them until they're ready.

If this sounds like something you'd take on, send me a DM.

We're running into a good problem right now. More leads coming in than we can efficiently handle.

Mostly new construction buyers in San Antonio and Austin, plus out-of-state relocations. The leads are solid but they need real work. They're warm, not hot. Most of them are three to six months away from actually moving.

Here's the part most agents won't do. They see a lead that isn't ready today and they move on. They want the buyer who's signing next week. I get it. But if you know how to nurture someone who's still in the research phase and actually turn them into a closed deal six months later, we have volume for you.

It takes patience. It takes a system. It takes follow up when they're not buying yet.

If this sounds like something you'd take on, send me a DM.

I started solo and thought the split was everything. Turned out it meant nothing without support. No one to call when a deal broke. No one to celebrate with when I won. I was making good money and miserable. Best lesson I learned. Build around people first. The money follows.

I hit a wall last month. Commission was solid but I was burnt out. Same routines. Same problems. No one pushing me to think bigger. I realized I wasn't growing anymore. I was just maintaining.

That's when I knew it was time to move.

If you're telling yourself you're fine where you are but you're not excited about tomorrow, that's a sign. If your broker hasn't invested in your growth in the last year, that's a sign. If you're making decent money but feel invisible, that's a sign.

Outgrowing a place doesn't mean the place is bad. It means you're ready for more.

The question isn't whether you should leave. It's whether you're brave enough to admit you've already left mentally?

I've been on teams where the broker didn't know my name and splits were all that mattered.

Now I lead differently. Our agents know they matter. When a deal gets messy, you've got people in your corner who actually care how it turns out. When you close something good, the whole team feels it. That's not soft stuff. That changes how you show up and what you're willing to push for. Agents stay because they're invested in something bigger than themselves. They work harder. They close more. They recommend other agents to us because they know what it feels like to be led by someone who has their back.

What does your broker know about you beyond your commission number?

Top earners don't work harder. They work different. They build systems that handle the repetitive stuff. They delegate what drains them. They show up every single day with a plan, not hope. The split doesn't matter if you're surrounded by people who push you to think bigger.

We closed more deals last month than the month before. Not because the market got better. Because the team got tighter.

When you're surrounded by agents who actually show up for each other, momentum builds different. You stop competing internally and start winning together.

What's keeping you from being part of something that grows?
